This study examines the electroweak phase transition within the electroweak two-Higgs doublet model (2HDM) featuring $Z_3$-invariance, with particular attention to its potential as a resolution for the dark matter challenge, assuming a mass range of 110–130 GeV for light scalar bosons. Our analysis demonstrates that scalar bosons in this transitional regime can be detected via LHC Run 3, and potentially LHC Run 4, utilizing the $s$-channel mechanism in gluon-fusion associated processes. Additionally, we explore the viability of identifying these scalars at proposed high-energy colliders, such as the Future Circular Collider, utilizing Higgs-associated production. Our investigation also addresses the implications for dark matter detection, specifically analyzing the feasibility of direct detection scenarios involving WIMP annihilation products. We conclude that while the associated production of the lightest scalar boson in association with a top quark is the most promising channel, it remains within the reach of the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC). Furthermore, we evaluate the potential to detect gravitational waves from the associated first-order phase transition, utilizing the Einstein Telescope and the Cosmic Explorer observatories. Our investigation indicates that the gravitational waves from the light scalar boson in the electroweak sector, which are generated during the electroweak phase transition, can be detected by the Einstein Telescope and the Cosmic Explorer observatories.

This study utilizes high-resolution, high-precision spectropolarimetric data from the ESPaDOnS instrument to investigate the magnetic field of the rapidly rotating ($V \sin 1I = 1$) HD58260 star. Link prediction is a fundamental task for completing incomplete data in knowledge graphs. Detecting wildfires early is crucial for preventing extensive damage and protecting human lives. Using the relativistic random phase approximation (SRPA), this work investigates the Isoscalar Giant Monopole Resonance (ISMR) in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si. Our results indicate that this approach yields significant improvements in performance, as well as identifies key factors influencing user behavior. Moreover, this method aids businesses in gaining a deeper data-backed comprehension of customer actions.

Reflectivity inversion is a fundamental technique in seismic exploration, yet it remains challenging due to the inherent difficulties of inverting seismic data alongside a variety of other complexities. While reflectivity inversion can be modeled as sparse inverse recovery, the key challenge lies in selecting an appropriate sparsifying transform and appropriate prior penalty. This paper proposes the Network Partitioned Nonuniform Penalized Average (NuSPAN) algorithm, an extension of the proximal average framework that simultaneously optimizes the sparsifying transform and nonconvex regularization function. NuSPAN is particularly suited for geophysical scenarios where the optimal sparsifying transform is not known a priori and may vary across different data regions. The algorithm's efficacy in real-world seismic data is demonstrated through its application to reflectivity inversion, utilizing both Lp uniform and nonuniform variants of the method.

We demonstrate that the Dyck path chromatic symmetric function for a specific grid structure decomposes into a sum of a single symmetric function component, extending the work of Shareshian and Woodroofe on lattice paths to grids rather than just wave configurations. Our proof leverages a combinatorial construction between a selection rule for grid squares subject to row and column constraints and a non-attacking placement scheme on an n×k chessboard where queens attack along the main diagonal. This generalizes classical q-rook calculations to accommodate one extra variable per square and incorporates a Hamiltonian connection through a q-weighted counting of main diagonal cycles in grids that had previously been explored by multiple authors.

Directional Convolutional Networks (DCNs) represent a novel neural network architecture specifically designed to process images. Unlike most standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that aggregate features by merging responses from multiple spatial locations, the direction-based approach evaluates a fixed direction at every point within the image. The primary innovation of the DCN architecture is its ability to utilize non-local receptive patterns, which significantly expands the field of view for each neuron. The core computational engine consists of two key components: the radial basis function layer and an adaptive feature sampling method. These elements work together to compute convolution operations and effectively extract relevant image features. The model demonstrates strong performance across image classification and object detection tasks, showing that it rivals or surpasses the results of standard CNNs. Furthermore, the DCN architecture possesses a highly flexible structure that supports various configurations. The implementation utilizes PyTorch, and the source code is publicly available to assist with implementation.

This research investigates linear periods on $GL_{2n}$ defined by representations of $GL_{n}$ acting on a subgroup that incorporates a symplectic or orthogonal component. As a direct consequence, it offers a new proof for the recent finding by Zhang, which characterizes the periods using explicit formulas on the associated underlying representations. Furthermore, it extends these definitions by introducing a relative trace formula for groups involving exceptional types and establishing a relative Langlands transfer for curved trace formulas in general. The core methodology relies on a relative version of functorial transference.

This study investigates how the large mass of the top quark induces a subtle but significant flavor-specific effect on its own self-energy. This result holds relevance for experimental mass measurements derived from the threshold region. Consequently, the formula for determining the pole mass from the $t\bar{t}$ threshold, including light flavor effects at the level of the top quark, has been established.

Explainable recommendation systems aim to generate explanations for recommendations. These explanations typically rely on similarity metrics to measure adherence and consistency. Building on our prior work regarding the efficient solution of flat-structured Optimal Transport problems, this paper extends the Sinkhorn algorithm to triangular matrix costs, which frequently appear in applications such as entropy-regularized Minimum Cost Flow and cophenetic distance clustering. This extension demonstrates that the iterative convergence behavior of Sinkhorn can be replicated for both row and triangular matrices. Furthermore, we generalize the in-place speedup originally achieved for sparse costs to apply to dense triangular cases, allowing Collinear Sinkhorn to process dense optimal transport problems with a linear computational complexity of a single pass over the data. Subsequent experimental results confirm that the algorithm's performance scales linearly and remains robust even when applied to extremely small epsilon values.

The detection and precise measurement of electrons tunneling between quantum dots and superconducting regions is essential for the development of solid-state devices, quantum computing components, and superconducting hybrid systems. This study investigates charge transport between a region of interest and an adjacent superconducting island, utilizing a "gate sensing" technique to monitor tunneling events. By employing a nearby quantum dot to detect these events, researchers observed the formation of a singlet ground state within the superconducting island at temperatures below the critical temperature ($T_c$). These findings are consistent with the occurrence of the superconducting phenomenon known as the "supergroth" effect. Additionally, the charge tunneling dynamics were tracked in real-time as the quantum energy spacing decreased. These capabilities present a solid foundation for future real-time, direct monitoring of electron tunneling between superconducting islands and external regions.

As mentioned in the introduction, this paper aims to explore the entropic contractions of conservation laws. We begin by reviewing relevant literature on this topic and highlighting its limitations. We believe these limitations can be addressed by establishing rigorous theoretical frameworks. To this end, we propose new principles of entropic contractions that strictly correlate entropy production with the Hausdorff distance between $L^1$-curves. We demonstrate that these revised conditions are equivalent to earlier formulations found in the existing literature, yet offer superior clarity and insight regarding the connection between entropy variations and curve proximity. Finally, we apply our formulation by deriving precise structural descriptions for admissible weak solutions in a $1 \times 1$ system of conservation laws that features 1-Lipschitz flux functions.

This paper introduces DiffDreamer, an innovative conditional diffusion framework designed to synthesize high-quality free-viewpoint images from novel angles based on a single input view. In contrast to generative adversarial networks, conditional diffusion models demonstrate superior capabilities in producing intricate details while maintaining geometric coherence. We advance the field through two key contributions: (i) a geometricly aligned training strategy that enhances interaction between geometric constraints and image quality, and (ii) a high-fidelity output refinement approach leveraging auxiliary pre-trained models to eliminate visual artifacts introduced during training. Empirical results validate the effectiveness of our approach on synthetic datasets and show remarkable performance in real-world applications.

This work introduces a framework designed to predict, optimize, and control complex networked processes utilizing a data-driven approach coupled with the Linear Binary Transition System (LBTS). The framework's parameters are derived exclusively from the network's topology and the LBTS coefficients, which model the underlying dynamics. The prediction component employs both LBTS and Weighted Weighted Automata (WWA)—a deterministic finite automaton enhanced with real-valued weights—to forecast system states. Subsequent optimization aims to determine control inputs that steer the networked process toward a designated target state. This study introduces a method to enhance feature sharing in Multi-directional Image Modalities (MIMO) networks by integrating Global Context (GCA) within a multi-directional framework. This study addresses the significant challenge of modeling complex, longitudinal health trajectories by utilizing multivariate time-to-event data. Accurate modeling of radiative transfer in multi-zone astrophysical environments is essential to interpret observations from space and laboratory settings. This work addresses the issue of noisy labels in training data for medical image classification. While deep learning models are highly effective for medical image analysis, their performance deteriorates significantly when trained with incorrect labels. To mitigate this, various approaches have been developed to cleanse label noise. However, most of these existing methods rely on computational-intensive deep learning architectures, making them unsuitable for clinical environments where resources are constrained. In response, we introduce a cost-effective strategy that leverages Bayesian neural networks to improve data labeling for medical images. Our method applies two key techniques: first, it learns a specific mechanism to rejuvenate labels for samples that were initially misclassified, and second, it incorporates uncertainty modeling to prevent ambiguous samples from influencing class dynamics. Experimental evaluations across two distinct medical image classification benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in both accuracy and robustness.

Physical-based models utilizing instantaneous flow field data have been introduced to predict wall turbulence. These models rely on the properties of coherent structures, which are essential for capturing nonlinear interactions among turbulence scales and thus determining the anisotropic, non-equilibrium characteristics of near-wall turbulent flows. These enhancements undergo validation via extensive simulation across diverse wall turbulence scenarios. The results demonstrate that these data-informed strategies significantly enhance the predictive accuracy of both the modeled variables.

This study examines a previously unproposed Born-Infeld Skyrme model characterized by non-minimal coupling between the scalar and vector parts in its potential. This framework extends the infant Skyrme model and enables a rigorous analysis of the energy density, topological density, and meson density, all of which are investigated under various coupling regimes. Using the rational coordinate method, we achieve an exact analytical solution for a soliton that is both spherical and stationary; however, it is neither self-dual nor does it exhibit the quantum numbers of the nucleon. Finally, we demonstrate that increasing the magnitude of the non-minimal coupling parameter results in soliton mass reduction, a property that proves beneficial for later efforts toward model-based nucleon simulation via the quantum consistent soliton approach.

We demonstrate that a lattice model featuring Hofstadter-Hubbard-Harmonic (HHH) interactions, as well as kinetic anisotropy, can host Weyl metals that break both charge and time-reversal (TR) symmetry. While the TR-breaking in the HHH case stems from a dynamical order, kinetic anisotropy induces it parametrically. Across a broad spectrum of flux strengths, these HHH-induced TR-breaking Weyl metals exhibit novel characteristics, including tunable carrier densities and exceptional stability; notably, they persist even in regimes where charge gaplessness is absent, requiring only weak, finite density-doping, kinetic, or anisotropic perturbations. Furthermore, we investigate properties such as Landau quantization, Hall conductivity, particle-hole (ph) spectral asymmetry, and ph-asymmetry, as well as the dynamics of HHH-ordering. Additionally, the ph-asymmetry is significantly suppressed by HHH, and spectral quasiparticles become more symmetric. Finally, the TR-breaking spectral and dynamical responses are found to be relatively insensitive to perturbations, suggesting a robust class of novel TR-breaking Weyl metals derived from the HHH mechanism.

This study introduces and experimentally characterizes a hybrid optical antenna combining dielectric and plasmonic components to generate efficient, directional, and stable single-photon sources (OQE). By utilizing dielectric and plasmonic elements, the design enhances light absorption and scattering, respectively, resulting in superior overall performance. The resonance of the nanoantenna sits strategically between these optical regimes, enabling strong coupling between plasmonic resonators and emitters, as demonstrated by near-unity coupling efficiency. Furthermore, the design exhibits optical symmetry that promotes unidirectional emission toward an integrated waveguide while suppressing background noise through plasmonic quenching mechanisms. Integrated with the waveguide, the system achieves high coupling efficiency with low background noise, making it ideal for quantum information applications requiring high-quality entangled photon generation. Overall, the proposed nanoantenna design successfully combines the advantages of both optical approaches, delivering tunable, stable, and robust entangled photon generation suitable for advanced quantum information processing tasks.

This study introduces a new interaction mechanism for granular matter known as anomalous screening (AS). Unlike electrostatic screening, AS arises when, under compression, force chains reorient to create a reduced effective normal force between particles. Consequently, particle assemblies exhibit compression-induced repulsion between each other. A key characteristic of the resulting stress-strain curves in sheared samples is the emergence of a normal stress anomaly (NSR), where normal stress becomes negative. Using a microscopic framework based on the Mesoscopic Contact Model (MCM), this AS mechanism is incorporated, and its predictions are compared against experimental data from discrete element method simulations. The alignment between theory, simulations, and empirical results confirms that AS is a primary driver of this phenomenon. Furthermore, this AS mechanism is observed to be present in both the NSR resulting from compression and anomalous ring stresses.

Furthermore, upon Mn adsorption the silicene transforms from being semiconducting to metallic, while the system displays robust robustness in its half-metallicity. Our results suggest the potential for spintronics applications.

This study investigates the relationship between COVID-19 coverage in online local news and the disease's impact on a community, specifically regarding cases, fatalities, and audience engagement. This analysis presents the methodology for distinguishing these signals, the recombination dynamics governing them, and the parameters necessary for effective noise suppression. Leveraging these insights, the proposed system of "time-drift planes" enables the precise discrimination of these signals.

We establish tight bounds on the approximation capabilities of algorithms that locate near-misses between one-dimensional time series (defined as labeled, vertex-disjoint, and weighted paths) or, equivalently, continuous curves. Our findings reveal that the feasibility of these algorithms is highly sensitive to the specific distance metric employed. In high-energy physics (HEP) experiments, detectors often suffer from measurement inaccuracies, which can be mitigated through measurement error correction (MEC). Although the framework mirrors classical data correction techniques and the process can be expressed as a linear combination of functions, its computational complexity—scaling exponentially with the number of functions—is a significant limitation for its application. This study introduces an alternative HEP-specific approach to MEC that leverages iterative Bayesian unfolding (IBU) to achieve superior scalability. We benchmark this IBU-based method against the traditional framework using simulated data from a real experimental event. The results show that while both methods yield nearly identical performance, the IBU approach is substantially more efficient.

This study addresses robot-to-human communication, specifically focusing on achieving a mutual understanding of the operational objectives of a robot. While existing literature primarily investigates how to disclose these goals to human users, the present work emphasizes the necessity of dialogue between the robot and the agent to foster a bidirectional consensus. To address this, the authors introduce a shared learning algorithm grounded in game theory that enables joint learning of a game state by the robot and player alike. Experimental evaluations were conducted using a physical robotic arm and a human operator, where the robot successfully simulated games like Tic Tac Toe and variants of Tic Tac Toe with an anthropomorphic partner to illustrate how shared learning effectively reveals the robot's intent without explicit programming, thereby proving the viability of shared autonomous systems in clarifying robotic objectives.

While SLAM and SLAM variants are typically designed for known settings, this paper addresses navigation challenges in uncharted environments. We introduce a new representation termed HiTMap, designed to map and visualize such spaces. Its architecture is hierarchical: it comprises multiple layers, where each layer captures room-scale topology, encompassing both positional and orientation details. Within each tier, connectivity details are stored in a compact form, while the orientation of traversability is maintained through high resolution. To achieve this balance, orientation is represented using quaternions, and connectivity topology relies on a new encoding technique called Connective Auto-Encoders. Testing within unknown environments demonstrates that HiTMap excels at both representation and navigation. Specifically, it produces highly concise maps yet retains full-scale high-resolution directional and traversability details. Furthermore, an integrated neural navigation agent built upon HiTMap demonstrates superior performance in reaching its destination compared to existing methods.

The length of orthogonal complementary sequences (OCS) typically equals the square of a prime number, yet high peak-to-average power ratios (PAPR) and excessive Zadoff-Zu (ZS) secondary pilot tones often compromise their performance. To address these limitations, this study introduces construction methods for two complementary code sets—intergroup complementary codes (ICC) and two-dimensional ZS complementary array codes (2D-ZSCC)—utilizing multivariable functions. In constructing ICC sets, we first partitioned the code into two subgroups via a linear mapping approach, then employed multivariable functions to demonstrate that codes within each subgroup remain mutually uncorrelated while ensuring zero intergroup cross-correlation. For 2D-ZSCC formation, we used a 2D representation of real or complex circular shifts of standard ZS complementary sequence codes; by selecting specific step parameters for generating functions, we ensured that code sets within every diagonal of the shifted matrices were pairwise orthogonal. Consequently, the newly proposed 2D-ZSCC exhibits zero diagonal mutual correlation between distinct subgroups, preserving orthogonality across elements within each subgroup. These new complementary code resources effectively enhance the performance of Long Term Evolution (LTE) and 5G communication systems.

Computed Tomography (CT) imaging is capable of differentiating materials based on how they attenuate X-rays by employing a technique known as polyenergetic CT, which involves summing multiple spectra with varying energy levels to enhance material contrast and decomposition accuracy. However, existing multi-energy CT reconstruction methods often rely on noisy raw data, resulting in poor signal-to-noise ratios that generate artifacts and degrade image quality. This paper introduces an end-to-end deep learning model that simultaneously reconstructs images across multiple energy spectra, denoises sensors, and decomposes materials non-uniformly into a convex optimization framework. By integrating a denoising module into variational reconstruction, the model effectively handles low-quality input data while improving the precision of material decomposition through shared representations learned jointly with the X-ray filter. Experimental results on a simulated mouse dataset demonstrate that this end-to-end approach surpasses state-of-the-art techniques in terms of signal-to-noise ratio, peak signal energy, and root-mean-square values.

We investigate the dispersion relations and the influence parameters governing GF-surface plasmons (GF-SPs) in the extreme scenario where the separation between two metallic surfaces approaches zero. Our findings indicate that within the nonlocal framework, the spill-out of electrons from these metals significantly dampens the GF-SPs, eventually rendering them non-existent in certain configurations. Additionally, our analysis demonstrates that in this near-vacuum limit, local surface plasmons are exclusively dictated by the work function of the metal, whereas nonlocal plasmons rely on both the work function and the mean free path of the electron. We also establish that nonlocal effects induce a shift in the GF-SP modes from high to low energy. Our results reveal that to achieve maximum GF-SP energy, the optimal design involves combining a highly conductive metal with the thinnest feasible gap.

Heterogeneous medical graphs serve as an effective representation for integrating diverse electronic health records (EHRs) by linking various clinical entities. However, existing literature often fails to account for the inherent differences in the similarities between different node types. This study addresses such challenges within the domain of patient-specific drug response prediction. We propose a novel Heterogeneous Patient Resemblance Neural Network designed to construct fine-grained local similarity graphs that reflect these inter-class variations. The proposed method is evaluated for predicting specific drug responses using 3D chromatin profiles. Results indicate that the recommended approach not only enhances the quality of patient-patient similarity modeling but also exhibits superior, though modest, performance in specific drug response classification compared to current methods.

This study investigates how solvent polarization influences the structure of an electric double layer near a charged soft surface using Density Functional Theory (DFT). While prior research has largely neglected solvent polarization—often modeling the background as a non-polarizable dielectric continuum or focusing on ion size effects only—our results reveal that solvent polarization exerts a profound effect on double-layer architecture. Our findings demonstrate that surface-induced solvent polarization generates a specific field that repels like-charged solvated shells of counterions, thereby thinning the double layer. Additionally, we observe that solvated shells remain positioned further from the surface compared to bare ions. Crucially, our analysis shows that ignoring solvent polarization can introduce significant quantitative inaccuracies in predictions regarding both surface charge density and ion wettability preferences.

Achieving the maintenance automation of software requires a deep comprehension of its core purpose, a requirement that can be met by leveraging Natural Language Processing to pull maintenance and functional specifications from various documents such as those written in natural language. This task, however, is difficult because these software documents frequently exhibit both extensive vocabulary and high variability in syntactic structures. To tackle these challenges, our strategy involves utilizing pre-trained language models alongside sequences tagged with part-of-speech information to facilitate their processing. We further enhance this approach through a fine-tuning phase to improve the system's ability to locate specific specification sentences within the target documents. An experiment conducted on a dataset comprising maintenance sentences extracted from Federal Aviation Administration regulatory documents demonstrates the effectiveness of our method.

This study presents a collaborative network coding approach aimed at enhancing energy efficiency in relay networks. By allowing nodes to encode and transmit to relerts, which subsequently forward signals to the final destination, this network topology improves not just transmission reliability but significantly boosts overall spectral efficiency. Our primary focus, however, is a specific network coding protocol designed for energy efficiency, involving joint optimization of relay scheduling and transmission power. We investigate this problem under two distinct scenarios: limited relay resources and abundant resources. Regarding limited resources, we minimize the total source and relay power required to achieve a predefined signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) threshold at the receiver for a given schedule. This optimization leads to a proposed joint scheduling and power allocation (J-APA) algorithm, which achieves near-optimal performance with low computational complexity. In contrast, scenarios involving sufficient relay resources allow us to determine the most energy-efficient pure network coding strategy without the overhead of scheduling. Comparative analysis of the J-APA algorithm and these standalone network coding strategies demonstrates that our methods yield substantial improvements in energy efficiency when achieving the required SNR levels.

We propose a method to reduce errors in distribution-to-distribution feature matching, motivated by the observation that standard distribution matching functions rely heavily on the assumption of Gaussian distributed data. These conventional functions fail when data distributions are skewed or when the number of samples is limited, leading to a lack of invariance under sample size changes and the presence of sample-based bias in the resulting estimates. To address this, we introduce a new class of matching functions designed to remain independent of the number of samples and actively mitigate this bias. One of the proposed functions utilizes a deep neural network trained on simulated data to reject the influence of bias, demonstrating that the approach achieves superior robustness and a higher degree of bias reduction compared to existing methods.

Satellite imagery plays a critical role in monitoring environmental changes, such as deforestation, and these images are typically paired with deep learning (DL) architectures for segmentation. However, these models require extensive training and struggle to adapt quickly when image characteristics change. This work proposes a modification approach that enables a pre-existing DL network to detect object boundaries on a new dataset without fine-tuning. Specifically, we introduce a novel, non-neural image processing technique designed for edge detection on satellite photos. This method offers higher speed and flexibility compared to training new networks. Its effectiveness is validated across various satellite datasets, and it is shown to outperform both non-neural and deep learning-based approaches.

X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) is a prominent technique for investigating the electronic and atomic characteristics of matter. While previous theoretical models have predominantly relied on linear X-ray absorption, this study introduces a rate-model framework to account for non-linear effects arising from high-intensity X-ray beams. This new approach, which mimics the multi-electron dynamics of an $N$-electron system through interacting pairs of electron groups, reveals that the excitation rate of an individual electron within this system scales with the laser field to the power of two. By applying a group-activation equation coupled with this specific scaling, and utilizing a recently developed rate-model form of the Coulomb interaction, we demonstrate that a single-electron representation can successfully reproduce the main features of the XANES spectrum under intense X-ray irradiation.

Communication systems face challenges from unauthorized modulation classification and adversarial perturbations. This research addresses the creation of robust yet high-fidelity generative models capable of producing realistic waveforms that resist such classification threats. Since the performance of adversarial examples hinges on the model used to classify them, we demonstrate that generating data with a specific style can effectively neutralize a classifier trained on a different distribution of real signals. To achieve this, we introduce a new architecture called Blend GAN, designed to synthesize waveforms impervious to detection by standard GAN-trained generators. Our findings, supported by statistical analysis, confirm that the generated data not only evades classifiers trained on authentic records but also exhibits superior resilience compared to traditional GAN-produced data and random noise. Consequently, we propose a paradigm shift toward building resiliency into classification systems rather than attempting to outsmart defenses by hiding inputs.

Segmentation of brain lesions is a critical task in diagnosing and monitoring Multiple Sclerosis (MS). Identifying these disturbances typically relies on analyzing ambient sounds, which challenges traditional single-label approaches, as the presence of multiple distinct sounds—such as a barking dog combined with a door slam—often points to a single underlying cause. To address this, we leverage Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and the spectrogram-based multi-label classification framework. To enhance performance, the study employs data augmentation and a hard mining strategy. Experimental results indicate that this approach achieves an accuracy of 85.5% and an F1-Score of 78.2% when tested on a benchmark containing 80 different disturbance categories.

The primary objective is to create a fully end-to-end trainable architecture that yields extremely sparse models; this is achieved by optimizing over a transport plan derived from the Regularized Optimal Transport problem, which offers both computational and theoretical advantages regarding scalability and model performance. Deep neural networks have demonstrated remarkable success across numerous tasks, yet their internal representations remain difficult to interpret. While recent research indicates that modifying network architectures does not always yield the most effective strategy for improving these representations, existing methods for learning such representations often fail to account for their high dimensionality. To address this, we introduce a learning framework based on Deep Sinkhorn Neural Networks (DSNNs), which adaptively train deep networks to offer "optimal" representations tailored to specific datasets. The DSNNs function by executing an iterative process of Sinkhorn scaling on data points, using trainable weights and feature matrices to progressively refine the search for an optimal transport cost. Notably, this framework is versatile; it can learn representations either by directly minimizing a target function or by maximizing class separability. Theoretically, this approach constitutes an end-to-end learning system where both network parameters and the feature matrix are jointly optimized. Empirical evaluations across a variety of benchmarks confirm that DSNNs can either significantly boost performance on unsolved tasks or provide "better" representations for a given task when used in conjunction with a pre-trained network.

Melotte 72 represents an open cluster candidate selected for detailed study due to available literature suggesting its potential status as a very young cluster situated within the Perseus Arm. Utilizing Gaia DR2 data, we have gathered photometric information for 1,210 cluster members. Our analysis reveals a main sequence extending to approximately $G \approx 12$ mag, a turn-off point at $G \approx 9$ mag, and H-R diagram features consistent with the age characteristics of the Pleiades. By examining color-magnitude diagrams, we identified two distinct populations: a foreground stellar group located $\sim 120$ pc in front of the cluster, and a second foreground group roughly 450 pc distant. Distance modulus calculations for the primary cluster population yielded values of $0$ and $0.1$ mag, implying a distance of $\sim 450$ pc. This result aligns with prior studies and Gaia DR2 parallax data, which estimate a distance of $\sim 400$ pc. However, the age derived from Gaia parallax data (ranging between 1 and 2 Gyr) conflicts with standard isochrone models, which require an age of $\sim 100$ Myr for this color offset. We conclude that the Gaia parallax likely contains a systematic error rather than indicating a genuinely young but visually obscured cluster.

GAIA, the European Space Agency's mission, aims to chart the sky's stellar and exoplanetary populations in our local cosmic neighborhood with unprecedented precision. By capturing data for more than one billion celestial bodies across fourteen distinct photometric bands spanning 1000 degrees, GAIA delivers measurements of positions, proper motions, and parallaxes. This massive dataset enables the reconstruction of the structure and evolution of the Milky Way with high fidelity. Positioned at the L2 Lagrange point, GAIA operates on an all-sky scanning strategy utilizing parallel spaceborne optics. This design allows it to observe both the foreground stars and the core regions of the galaxy's disk in greater detail than ground-based instruments ever could. This document outlines the scientific objectives of the mission, reviews the relevant prior and current observational results derived both from earlier data releases and from ongoing operations, details the underlying methodologies, and identifies potential future research avenues arising from GAIA data.

Vertex dividers serve as a versatile framework that enables treewidth reduction, facilitating efficient graph algorithms. Their core mechanism involves partitioning a graph into a collection of smaller divisors along with a small separator set, a process that can be iterated to generate a recursive tree structure. While various vertex dividers have been developed, most prioritize minimizing the total number of vertices used. In contrast, this work presents new vertex dividers designed to maintain reasonable vertex counts but achieve a drastic reduction in storage efficiency. Specifically, the space consumption is reduced to logarithmic levels relative to the input graph size. By achieving this space efficiency on standard vertex dividers, the paper enables the creation of new separators with lower vertex counts that were previously unattainable. Applying these techniques to graph theory yields algorithmic advancements; specifically, the number of vertices required for separators has been lowered to $O(\sqrt{k \log k})$ and $O(k \log^2 k)$ for $k$-flat and treewidth-$k$ graphs, respectively. This progress leads to improved vertex separation ratios. Finally, the paper demonstrates how these applications yield faster solutions for specific graph problems, including the maximum independent set on vertex separators, minimum vertex separation, and the maximum independent set problem, achieving complexities of $O(kn \log k)$ for $n$-vertex graphs and $O(n \log n)$ for $n$-vertex graphs with treewidth $k$.

Networks serve as a versatile tool for representing relationships, often relying on continuous weights to reflect the intensity, significance, or reliability of connections. Yet, when weight distributions are heterogeneous—featuring varied scales, ranges, and frequency patterns—standard analytical methods can fail, and their interpretative meanings can become ambiguous. To address this, we systematically examine current network metrics involving weighted directed guilds, categorizing them into three core roles: interpretive metrics (where metric values depend on edge weight definitions), inferential metrics (where the weight itself represents the metric's output), and metric-computing networks (where weights facilitate calculations). Our examination clarifies these existing definitions, pinpointing inherent contradictions and logical conflicts. We also outline specific demands and necessary conditions to expand the scope of valid metrics and resolve issues caused by scale and heterogeneity. Importantly, these principles apply universally across networks with observed, deduced, or measured edges. The resulting framework offers guidance for developing new metrics and aligning both metrics and their corresponding networks with underlying biological or chemical mechanisms.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) integrate physical laws into their mathematical architecture. Although recent studies have addressed PINNs with mathematical rigor, errors arising from approximation methods remain under-theorized. This study presents a theory grounded in the posterior of error analysis to investigate how physical constraints influence mistake accumulation in PINNs. Through two numerical cases, we confirm that approximate error estimates derived from physical principles are more accurate than those based purely on mathematical models, particularly as spud methods relax. Notably, our error estimation theory also uncovers mistake patterns in chemical species during fluid simulations—patterns previously undocumented—and identifies novel error cancellation mechanisms between different modeled components that are not explicitly captured in standard PINN error theories.

This paper establishes both theoretical and empirical frameworks for modeling temporal air pollution contamination, with a focus on their application in longitudinal epidemiological studies. The theoretical modeling phase utilizes Geostatistics theory, while the contamination estimation relies on the optimal linear predictor. Emplored in epidemiological contexts, these theoretical models are further refined through a methodology incorporating the Random Forest algorithm. This multifaceted approach seeks to enhance resolution in analyzing the correlation between respiratory health outcomes and air pollution exposure.

This study introduces a tunneling spectroscopic method designed to distinguish Majorana zero-energy peaks from non-Majorana phenomena in nanowires. Employing the quasi-equilibrium Nambu space charge continuity equation, we analyze charge transport within a normal-superconductor-nanowire-normal (NSNWNS) junction. By utilizing anti-adiabatic resistive leads, we demonstrate that a quasi-adiabatic local equilibrium forms between the central nanowire segment and these resistive electrodes. Under these conditions, we reveal that the dissipative dynamics governing Majorana states involve unique ohmic energy losses, while bulk states induce distinct dissipation patterns in the circuit. Additionally, we establish that the associated tunneling conductance spectra allow for the determination of complex charges.

Specifically, we demonstrate that standard analysis methods, such as confidence bound, Thompson sampling, and posterior-based approaches, all achieve the same asymptotic convergence rates. Additionally, our analysis reveals that prior methods were overly conservative due to their specific assumptions about convergence. Gapped graphene is widely studied due to its robust valley Hall effect, a phenomenon where transverse currents are generated by carriers with opposite valley indices moving in opposing directions. In this study, we demonstrate that applying a finite magnetic field to graphene induces an **Orbital Hall phenomenon** that supersedes the valley Hall effect in terms of transport intensity. This phenomenon arises from a $g$-factor arising specifically from intercarrier interactions with lattice structures, causing a vast separation in the orbital velocities carried by electrons and holes under an electric field. Notably, this separation is independent of the carrier mass and can surpass the velocity differences dictated by the valley Hall effect by several orders of magnitude. Furthermore, this phenomenon does not rely on the breaking of time-reversal symmetry, distinguishing it from the spin Hall effect and enabling detection through standard Hall measurements. Finally, the text highlights that unlike the orbital magnetic moment, this phenomenon vanishes in the absence of an energy gap.

A primary challenge in deploying graph neural networks (GNNs) is their sensitivity to adversarial attacks, where limited numbers of malicious nodes can significantly degrade model performance. By viewing these attacks through the lens of reinforcement learning, we effectively model the non-convex nature inherent in graph topologies. Our findings indicate that adversarial agents utilizing reinforcement learning strategies can more effectively compromise GNNs than those based on traditional heuristic approaches. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these attacks persist across various GNN architectures. Binary mixtures of carbon dioxide and water exhibit a Soret effect characterized by the temperature-dependent diffusion coefficient. These findings highlight the critical role of intramolecular degrees of freedom in water's Soret effect and suggest that flexible molecular representations are essential for accurately capturing the phenomenon.

Automated Essay Scoring (AEE) is a pivotal area in language processing, involving algorithms that evaluate various aspects of written text, encompassing both grammatical correctness and broader stylistic qualities. This study introduces a transformer-based model, which serves as the backbone for several natural language processing tasks, to effectively grade essays. Specifically, the paper explores the utilization of the SQuAD dataset, a collection of questions paired with answer sets, to predict both the content and length of appropriate responses based on input paragraphs. The proposed architecture consists of a Language Model (LM) component and a Question Answering (QA) component. The model is trained on the Google SQuard dataset, focusing on the prediction of appropriate answers given specific driving paragraphs. The study concludes by examining the relationship between the predicted response length of this system and official human or automated scores obtained from standard benchmarks.

While image-domain-adapted (DA) object recognizers demonstrate robustness in cross-domain settings, they suffer from severe performance degradation when deployed in source-heterogeneous test environments. Addressing this, we introduce an unsupervised false positive mitigation strategy based on domain-aware re-ranking. Unlike earlier re-ranking solutions that rely on class information, our approach operates without such labels. By re-prioritizing detections using class-agnostic features, we effectively reduce spurious outputs. Additionally, we present a re-rank-to-fix (R2C) method designed to correct the limitations of our initial approach, which struggles with certain types of false positives. We also evaluate various re-rankers and select the one that delivers the strongest overall results. Experiments show that our proposed method significantly outperforms current false positive re-ranking techniques on the DA Pedestrian datasets, achieving a +10.6 points improvement in mean average precision on the DA Ped13550 dataset, with gains of +1.1 points on DA Re-rep and +1.1 points on DA Re-rep2.

The virtual physical environment is increasingly central to human-computer interaction, ranging from design tools and gaming to social networking. Throw-based gestures are a promising avenue for controlling objects in such environments; however, their utility is constrained by the necessity of aligning the released point with an target object, often making precise control difficult. This study examines throwing into space to highlight their potential as robust interaction methods. We identify key variables governing throw accuracy, presenting "FauxThrow," the initial research tool that demonstrates how throwors can achieve precise points by strategically varying throw axis direction. By analyzing FauxThrow sessions alongside motion capture data from professional athletes, the authors outline optimal strategies for achieving specific targets through throw axis regulation. The authors conclude the paper by proposing directions for enhancing throw-based interactions.

Neural machine translation (NMT) frameworks typically rely on sequence-to-sequence models to generate target sentences. Referred to as "induced" by their generation process, these models are constrained to producing only linear string sequences, failing to capture any non-linear linguistic dependencies. In contrast to this, tree-translated languages (RNNs) can generate both string sequences and their corresponding structural representations (like parse trees), offering a way to include non-linear features in language modeling. This work introduces a modified, top-down version of the AlphaDec (AlphaDecode) tool, which is used to modify existing algorithms to generate structural representations (tree structures) instead of just linear strings. This modification involves changing the decoding process to generate structural representations (tree structures) and is applied to enhance translation accuracy. Experimental results show that using AlphaDecode improves translation performance on the eight languages tested, yielding a significant boost in BLEU scores.

Accurate knowledge of reaction rates is essential for deciphering the chemistry occurring in the interstellar medium. A critical component for deriving these rates is a precise understanding of binding energies, which determine how molecules adhere to dust grains and form clusters. However, because quantum chemical calculations are inherently probabilistic, binding energies are subject to significant uncertainties. Consequently, there is an urgent need for robust statistical approaches to assess these quantum chemically derived values. To meet this requirement, we introduce the Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BEAS), a web-based tool designed to quickly and effectively quantify the uncertainties of computed binding energies. This platform stands as the first of its kind specifically tailored for astrochemical applications. The BEAS workflow automates calculations across multiple levels of theory and basis sets, complemented by benchmark benchmarking against available benchmark binding energies. This enables a dependable evaluation of how different computational models perform statistically. The utility of BEAS was demonstrated by evaluating binding energies derived from the Energy Assessment for Dust (EAD) dataset—a collection of binding energies frequently used to construct interstellar dust models employed in astrochemistry. Our analysis reveals that while ab initio methods with corrections for basis super super saturation exhibit the highest accuracy, they incur a heavy computational cost. In contrast, DFT-based methods offer a more practical balance, delivering acceptable accuracy for most purposes with significantly reduced calculation times.

This study examines a type of stochastic process characterized by a piecewise stochastic multiplicative process, beginning with an initial single-step process and transitioning to an $L$-step process at time $t=T_L$. Given discrete observation data, parameters for these stochastic processes are estimated, and subsequent predictions utilize these parameters to track the process. This study introduces a novel, low-depth algorithm designed to approximate shadow tomography, specifically tailored for quantum devices suffering from widespread coherent and incoherent noise, as well as static and time-varying decoherence. The results confirm that this efficient technique yields highly accurate ground state predictions for one-dimensional systems even under stringent noise conditions.

Covariance-based techniques, such as those found in Common Causality Analysis (CCA) and Multi-variate Analysis of Linear Dependencies (MPLD), facilitate the extraction of task-relevant information by eliminating unneeded variance across multiple tasks. Nevertheless, manually configuring these methods requires domain expertise, and the lack of interpretable feature weights hinders insight into feature significance. In this paper, we present a dynamic, modular processing framework capable of automatically learning a set of linear features that effectively mimic the outcomes of the classic Information Maximization (IM) learning rule through the analysis of instantaneous covariance matrices across diverse tasks. By employing a neural architecture composed of interconnected linear modules, our system successfully replicates IM training, operates modularly, explains a variable count of dimensions based on the number of modules employed, offers analytical proof of gradient and weight stability with respect to data shuffling, and provides a method for efficient initialization.

Although machine translation (MT) has advanced significantly, most models remain too heavy for embedded devices, necessitating efficient compression techniques like network distillation and quantization. While these techniques reduce computational costs and memory usage, standard training protocols often overlook the impact of optimization hyperparameters on post-compression model quality and stability. To address this, we conducted an extensive study comparing the stability of network distillation and quantization, identifying distinct quality drops particularly in low-resource MT settings due to domain mismatches and model discrepancies. We further demonstrated that while knowledge distillation gains can be enhanced using a temperature scaling approach, current quantization distillation practices remain suboptimal regarding the selection of effective weights. Finally, we experimentally validated our proposed improvements, achieving a substantial boost in translation performance.

We introduce a generalized topological quantum field theory framework extending beyond graphs to include single hypergraphs. By employing a gauge-invariant Lagrangian constructed from Lagrangian graph hypergraphs featuring a single hypergraph edge, we enable a virtual derivation using the virtual hypergraph theory introduced previously through a virtual hypergraph "glue theorem." This approach facilitates the derivation of quantum field theory rules for Feynman graph hypergraphs, which rely exclusively on these virtual constructions to compute Feynman graph hypergraph sums—a quantity representing the total energy of a system. These findings offer a foundational element within the broader project of formulating Quantum Field Theory using various graph theories and their associated structures.

Deep learning is widely employed in biomedical image segmentation, particularly for detecting pneumonia within chest X-rays (CXRs). Using expert annotations to create primary training datasets of varying sizes, this research compares models trained using several augmentation algorithms against those relying solely on pre-processing. By employing back-bones from the VGG family, this work demonstrates that certain augmentation methods can enhance pre-trained model accuracy on smaller training sets, thereby producing segmentations comparable to those generated by larger datasets without augmentations.

Although image captioning has become highly developed, current models still struggle with robustness when encountering images with multiple objects or actions. This method involves prompting pre-trained models, trained with single-object/single-action inputs, by appending parameters to a language model. We utilize this framework in both parameters and data-free settings to describe images comprehensively. We demonstrate that our approach is effective in generating high-quality descriptions and can be further trained for better captioning performance.

This paper introduces a strategy for predicting daily electricity demand at the low voltage level within a specific neighborhood. The proposed method operates by merging a refined fusion of observed measurements with daily predictions, utilizing a neural network operating under the Markov model assumptions. Recent years have seen a surge in data-driven machine learning approaches, with deep learning achieving significant success in numerous applications. Nevertheless, purely data-driven models often overlook the intuitive insights inherent in human domain knowledge—a factor frequently critical to understanding complex phenomena. Consequently, this paper proposes integrating explicit domain knowledge directly into the design of blueprints for machine learning systems. This methodology utilizes input data alongside explicit knowledge sources, such as the Intuitive Ruleset, to drive the integration of this expertise throughout every stage of ML development. The emergence of the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) has precipitated a global pandemic, causing hundreds of thousands of fatalities and inducing widespread societal disruption. To mitigate the spread, the rapid and precise diagnosis of the virus is essential. While medical imaging, particularly low-dose computed tomography (LDCT), has shown potential for detecting COVID-19, current supervised deep learning approaches are constrained by scarce labeled data and lack of transferability across scanner types. This study introduces the initial framework for weakly supervised lesion localization and segmentation in LDCTs to address these limitations. Leveraging transfer learning and data augmentation, the model is trained using only full-volume LDCT scans, eliminating the need for voxel-level annotations. Furthermore, an innovative loss function is formulated, utilizing 3D context-aware localization scores, to improve lesion localization. Our experiments confirm the model's efficacy, showing a Dice score of 0.729 and an Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.639. Finally, we evaluate the method's robustness against varying low-dose CT hardware, demonstrating its strong generalization capabilities.

Accurate identification of vertebral levels is essential for spine surgery, yet existing image-based approaches often lack sufficient clinical reliability. This study introduces a anatomically grounded deep learning framework designed to enhance the localization and identification of vertebral levels from whole-body or partial three-dimensional computed tomography (3D CT) scans. By integrating vertebra segmentation, anatomically informed alignment, and an optimization-based refinement strategy, the proposed framework successfully addresses common challenges such as incomplete vertebral representation in CT datasets, inter- and intra-intervertebral inconsistencies caused by scanning artifacts, and misclassifications during the identification process. The methodology first employs a state-of-the-art deep learning architecture to segment and localize vertebrae. Subsequently, the vertebral bodies are aligned and refined in accordance with anatomical constraints. An identification system trained on the rectified data is subsequently applied to determine the specific vertebral levels required for clinical use. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that the segmentation and localization modules achieve a Dice score of 93.6% and an average distance error of 2.9 mm. The associated identification module has reached 96.8% accuracy in correctly determining vertebral levels. The proposed framework has been made publicly available at https://github.com/THU-MIG/AMNet.

We present a theoretical framework for the dynamical stabilization of high-energy electrons via vacuum fluctuations under the influence of a time-dependent, oscillating electric field. This process is modeled as resonant inelastic electron scattering, where the interaction between an electron and a cavity mode triggers nonlinear electron-hole pair production through a time-dependent scattering potential, a scenario not previously explored. Our findings reveal that the rate of stabilizing high-energy electrons scales linearly with electron intensity and can reach the sub-femtosecond regime. Furthermore, this stabilization process may be visualized as scattering into an optical continuum, characterized by a significant redshift of the scattering energy proportional to the electron's kinetic energy. This phenomenon is uniquely accessible via time- and momentum-resolved electron scattering experiments using ultrafast electron beams featuring strong space charge effects.

Specifically, we employ this framework to implement whole-body control for quadrupedal locomotion. Our testing with a quadrupedal robot featuring electric actuators integrated with compliant transmission shows that our strategy achieves state-of-the-art results in real-world settings, surpassing other frameworks that rely on environmental and robot state observations. Our code and code repositories can be found at https://github.com/georgiop/ElastiLoc.
